extracted.intended_audience: Shakespeare scholars, textual editors, and graduate students in English literature
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles (explicit and implicit) for producing and assessing editions and criticism of Shakespeare's works, with attention to eighteenth-century editorial practice and literary-critical criteria. Focuses on Rowe's 1709 edition and its place in editorial and critical history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial modernization (spelling and punctuation) and sensible emendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rowe 'modernized spelling and punctuation and quietly made a number of sensible emendations.' It is described as the first 'edited' edition because of these practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should modernize orthography and punctuation where it aids comprehension, and make emendations judged sensible; such unobtrusive changes can restore passages and be accepted by subsequent editors. Balance is required to avoid over-altering the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of dramatis personae
rubrics_metrics.description: Rowe's edition is 'the first edition to include dramatis personae.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide cast lists/ dramatis personae for each play to help readers identify characters and their relations; this is a feature of an editorially helpful edition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic division into acts and scenes, with distinct scene locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rowe was 'the first to attempt a systematic division of all the plays into acts and scenes, and the first to give to scenes their distinct locations.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should impose clear act/scene divisions and indicate locations to improve usability and comprehension for readers, unless strong textual evidence argues otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Rowe's edition was 'the first of many illustrated editions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider adding illustrations to make the edition more attractive and to aid reader engagement; illustrations are a legitimate editorial device to broaden appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and accessibility (abandoning folio for more convenient formats)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rowe 'abandoned the clumsy folio format and attempted to bring the plays within reach of the understanding and the pocketbooks of the average reader.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose formats (e.g., octavo, duodecimo) that increase physical accessibility and affordability for a broader readership; format decisions are part of editorial responsibility to readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of extended biographical and critical material
rubrics_metrics.description: Rowe's edition is 'the first to include an extended life and critique of the author.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a biography and critical introduction to situate the author and works historically and critically. Be aware that biographical material may mix fact and tradition — signal uncertainties and separate lore from documented fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of an established textual base combined with editorial judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Rowe's edition was 'based substantially on the Fourth Folio (1685),' but he also made editorial changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin from an authoritative base text but apply careful emendation and judgment; document textual decisions so later scholars can evaluate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious, unobtrusive commentary and restoration (avoid 'pomp of notes')
rubrics_metrics.description: Johnson praised Rowe for doing 'more than he promised; and that, without the pomp of notes or the boast of criticism, many passages are happily restored.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor restoring and clarifying text over heavy-handed annotation; unobtrusive editorial action that clarifies the text can be preferable to excessive notes that draw attention away from the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing the plays for contemporary taste and comprehensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Rowe 'helped to make [Shakespeare] comprehensible within the framework of contemporary taste' and restated Dryden's view to make works readable and admired despite formal objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and critics should consider contemporary readers' expectations and tastes when presenting works, explaining features that might otherwise appear objectionable, while making clear where modern tastes differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fact from tradition in biographical material
rubrics_metrics.description: The text notes that Rowe 'assembled the few facts and most of the traditions' about Shakespeare and that 'scholarship...has demonstrated the unreliability of most of the local traditions that Betterton reported.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including biographical anecdotes and local traditions, clearly indicate evidential status; separate well-attested facts from oral tradition or conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial revision and selection of prefatory material (rearrangement/omission of outmoded or erroneous passages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pope 're-arranged the material, giving it a more orderly structure and omitting passages that were obviously erroneous or that seemed outmoded.' Later editors often relied on such revisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefatory and critical apparatus may be revised for clarity and relevance; editors may omit demonstrably erroneous or obsolete remarks but should record such changes and the rationale for later scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary-criticism criteria — virtues to emphasize
rubrics_metrics.description: Rowe (following Restoration criticism and Dryden) emphasizes Shakespeare's virtues: images 'so lively,' command over the passions (especially terror), 'magic' or the supernatural, the creation of varied and convincing characters, and depiction of 'manners.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical accounts should highlight vivid imagery, emotional power, supernatural elements, and character-drawing as central merits of Shakespeare's dramaturgy; use examples (e.g., Falstaff) to illustrate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary-criticism criteria — faults to acknowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay records commonly cited faults: 'incorrect in grammar; ... sank to flatness or soared into bombast; his wit could be coarse and low and too dependent on puns; his plot structure was at times faulty, and he lacked the sense for order and arrangement that the new taste valued.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A balanced critique should admit deficiencies (grammar, occasional bombast, coarse wit, reliance on puns, plot irregularities, neglect of classical unities) even while affirming the writer's genius; such faults inform editorial and interpretive choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of mode of reception: reading vs stage performance
rubrics_metrics.description: The text notes different receptions of plays in reading ('Shakespeare read as opposed to Shakespeare seen') and suggests that romantic comedies might fare better read privately than staged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess works both as texts for readers and as pieces for performance; some plays may be better appreciated in one medium than another, and editorial commentary should address these differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in attribution and authenticity assessments
rubrics_metrics.description: Rowe 'refused to determine the genuineness of the 1640 poems' and later editors handled attribution differently; the account warns about dubious traditions and spurious works being collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise caution and evidence-based methods when attributing works; avoid definitive claims without strong documentary support; document uncertainties regarding authorship or genuineness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefatory tone and organization as critical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Rowe's preface is described as 'loosely organized, discursive, intimate, and ... contagious enthusiasm' modeled on Dryden; Johnson called the preface lacking 'much profundity or penetration.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefatory materials may adopt an approachable, discursive tone to engage readers, but should balance enthusiasm with critical depth; choice of tone influences how readers receive the edition.
